title: Man charged after Hackney attacks on three Jewish women
description: A 33-year-old man has been charged after three Jewish women were assaulted in Hackney, east London.Police were called to Clapton Common at about 13:40
body: A 33-year-old man has been charged after three Jewish women were assaulted in Hackney, east London.Police were called to Clapton Common at about 13:40 BST on Monday following reports that a man had been detained by Shomrim, a Jewish neighbourhood watch group, after assaulting the women.The victims suffered minor injuries.Abdisamad Siad, of Pilgrims Way, Islington, has been charged with three counts of assault by beating. He is due to appear at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court later.The Metropolitan Police said it had increased its patrols in the local area since the incident.The force said it was also working with Jewish community leaders to provide "further reassurance" to those living nearby.Siad has also been charged with grievous bodily harm with intent over an unrelated attack on a woman, who is believed to be known to him, in the Islington area on 16 October.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain
description: The decision to grant approval for drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea and the further delay in a decision about the Rosebank oil field
body: The decision to grant approval for drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea and the further delay in a decision about the Rosebank oil field, also in the North Sea, are case studies in the slow-motion awkwardness the UK has collectively had, over years, about energy.At the heart of that awkwardness, these questions: where should our energy come from, and with what costs and consequences, for the customer and for the environment?Since becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham has talked about a desire to be "pragmatic" about the North Sea as he puts it, which is why this decision about Jackdaw isn't a surprise.In fact it felt near inevitable after President Trump blurted out – after his first phone call with Burnham in the summer – that the prime minister had told him he would "open up the North Sea".Burnham acknowledged the two leaders had discussed the issue, arguing: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that."What we now know is the government is approving drilling of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen. A decision on Rosebank, an oil field about 80 miles north east of Shetland, is expected to take a bit longer.The timeline of back and forth about both projects is worth revisiting. Jackdaw was first approved four years ago, Rosebank three years ago. But after a legal challenge by environmental campaigners, it was ruled that consent had been granted unlawfully and there needed to be a more detailed assessment of the environmental impact.And then, of course – there is politics, international and domestic, between parties and within parties. Debate about energy security and spiralling prices, given the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the environmental impact, carbon emissions and the message new drilling sends to the wider world.But others point to the extra carbon emissions when energy is imported, the tax revenues generated from domestic energy and the social and economic consequences of the British oil and gas sector deindustrialising too quickly and, in particular, the impact on cities such as Aberdeen.Then, for the government, there are the promises the Labour Party made when it was seeking your support at the general election in 2024.Page 52 of Labour's manifesto reads like a rhetorical twister – a paragraph of promises seeking to stretch in multiple directions at the same time, trying to keep a breadth of people happy simultaneously, or perhaps not annoy too many people too much."Labour will not revoke existing licences and we will partner with business and workers to manage our existing fields for the entirety of their lifespan. Crucially, oil and gas production in the North Sea will be with us for decades to come, and the North Sea will be managed in a way that does not jeopardise jobs," it reads."And our offshore workers will lead the world in the industries of the future. We will not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure, and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis," it adds.Crucially, the Jackdaw and Rosebank licences had already been issued, leaving political wriggle room on these two outstanding and high profile decisions the Labour government inherited on taking office.But the multiple trade-offs, of course, remain very real, including for some of the key individuals involved. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who used to be the energy secretary, has long been vocal about what he sees as the need to move away from fossil fuels.His successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh, who has announced this decision, previously wrote, external that "to have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can't have any new oil or gas fields," adding "it's irresponsible and short sighted to be funding new fossil fuels when we need to get to Net Zero fast."Fahnbulleh has today told BBC Radio Scotland gas from Jackdaw will be "in our homes and businesses this month" but acknowledged that it "won't lower our energy bills this winter".Instead, she is grounding her argument for approving this in energy security and saying the tax revenue generated will go into an "Energy Wealth Fund" to pay for "low carbon and renewable projects".Rosebank, she added, was a "different proposition" as its oil would be exported, but she will "look at it".Politically, the decision on Jackdaw is considerably easier for the government than the decision on Rosebank. Broadly speaking, most Labour MPs are comfortable with endorsing Jackdaw. It is also a project backed by the Conservatives and Reform (who argue a decision should have been taken much sooner) and the Scottish National Party and the Liberal Democrats. The Green Party of England and Wales are opposed.On Rosebank, the argument is much more contentious within the Labour Party. Some, who can see the rationale for Jackdaw cannot see it for Rosebank. Bluntly, it is a much more difficult decision, as Fahnbulleh has acknowledged.What we can expect in the coming hours and days - as it has started already - is a resumption of all the arguments these projects have already provoked, with some saying approval should have happened ages ago, alongside plenty more. And others arguing the announcement is utterly irresponsible.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain

title: Woman told she had cancer by data-breaching hospital worker
description: A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee who accessed her record days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant.Pip
body: A woman was told she had cancer by a hospital employee who accessed her record days before she was due to receive test results from her consultant.Pippa Boardman, from Lostwithiel in Cornwall, said she had lost her dignity and privacy through the data breach at the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro. She said she did not receive an apology from the hospital until it was contacted by the BBC.The trust said it was "truly sorry" and "appropriate action had been taken".It added: "While we cannot disclose the details of individual employment matters, we want to reassure Ms Boardman that we have treated this extremely seriously."Boardman, who is now recovering well from cancer, said her personal information was accessed by a man she vaguely knew who worked at the hospital.She said: "I got a phone call at home from somebody I know through the sport that I play. "This man said to me 'Pippa, I don't want you to worry, but you've got cancer'."I just couldn't really believe it".Two days later Boardman was told by her consultant she did have breast cancer.Nine months on, she said her strong recovery did not undo the damage done by the experience, adding: "I lost my dignity and I've lost my privacy."Along with Boardman's case there have also been other recent NHS data breaches, described by Health Secretary Yvette Cooper as a disgrace.Boardman said part of her trauma had been caused by the Royal Cornwall Hospital's handling of the case.She said: "It really distresses me people can't see just how invasive and intrusive it is if somebody looks at your information and then shares it inappropriately."She said the trust told her the breacher's rights meant it could not give her information, and it only apologised after being contacted by the BBC.She said: "It took a lot of courage to complain... and I didn't understand why the hospital wasn't really prepared to engage with me."I understand that it's because his rights have to be protected. But I kept thinking where are my rights in this."Boardman said she wanted to prevent others going through a similar experience."I'm in a very good place in terms of my cancer. I'm just in an awful place in terms of what happened and how it happened," she said.The Royal Cornwall Hospital Trust said it was "truly sorry" about how Boardman was contacted.It said: "Whilst the member of staff had legitimate access to her records as part of their work, it was outside of their role to contact her."This should not have happened and we recognise the distress and concern it will have caused."Appropriate action was taken following our investigation which was carried out immediately after Ms Boardman raised her concern." The trust said it had reminded staff records "must only ever be accessed for a legitimate work-related reason" and it was also reviewing policies "in light of the strengthened NHS England guidance on inappropriate access to patient information".

schema.headline: Woman told she had cancer by data-breaching hospital worker

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Burnham faces climate revolt' and 'Harry wants to fix feud'
description: The Guardian says Andy Burnham will face a "climate revolt" by approving drilling at the Jackdaw gas field., external The paper says that, while it wi
body: The Guardian says Andy Burnham will face a "climate revolt" by approving drilling at the Jackdaw gas field., external The paper says that, while it will be a "major boost" for Britain's oil and gas industry, critics will argue it undermines Labour's green credentials. According to the Financial Times, ministers are expected to say that the project will help increase energy supplies this winte, externalr. The i Paper reports that it will be able to power around a million UK homes., externalThe Times reports that the home secretary is facing pressure from her cabinet colleagues to water down plans, external which would make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK. But an ally of Shabana Mahmood tells the paper that Burnham is "on her side" and is "holding the line". "Mahmood's fight to save her migrant crackdown" is the headline.The Daily Telegraph says a review of anti-Semitism in schools in England is expected to prompt some to ban teachers from wearing pro-Palestinian badges. , externalAccording to the Guardian, the report by Sir David Bell finds that three in five Jewish students have been affected, external by anti-Semitism.The decision to deploy RAF jets to defend Saudi Arabia is described by the Times as an "expansion of the UK's role in the conflict in Yemen", external. A defence source tells the paper that "if Houthi drones or missiles come over the border" then British jets will "take them out". The Telegraph's verdict is: "Better late than never".The Daily Mirror leads with the Covid inquiry's findings that government failures during the pandemic allowed the virus to "spread like wildfire" in care homes., external In its leader column, the paper says care home residents were "shamefully abandoned by those entrusted with protecting them".Prince Harry's call for reconciliation with his father and brother is the focus of the Sun's front page, external. It says the Duke of Sussex is hoping to "fix his bitter family feud". But the Daily Mail accuses him of "reopening old wounds" in what it describes as a "new Sussex psychodrama", external. Its headline reads: "Oh, do put a sock in it, Harry!".

title: Ali G is back. But is Sacha Baron Cohen's character past its sell-by date?
description: "This is the biggest gathering of cultural appropriators in history," Sacha Baron Cohen tells the camera in his parody of a street accent.Behind him,
body: "This is the biggest gathering of cultural appropriators in history," Sacha Baron Cohen tells the camera in his parody of a street accent.Behind him, hundreds of fans cram onto a London Underground escalator, all wearing Ali G's trademark yellow shell suit and skullcap. Baron Cohen shouts the character's catchphrases through a megaphone, with the crowd enthusiastically finishing each one.Earlier this month, more than 300 fans attended an official Ali G lookalike competition, ferried around London on an open-top bus that stopped at landmarks including Big Ben, Leicester Square and Covent Garden.The stunt was promotion for an upcoming sequel to 2002 film Ali G Indahouse - called Ali G: Who iz I? - which hits cinemas on Friday.But not everyone is excited about the return of Baron Cohen's comedy character. Critics have long accused the actor of perpetuating racial stereotypes with Ali G, and criticism of the upcoming sequel has gained traction online, with social media posts from comedians, content creators and film fans attracting thousands of likes and comments. Among them is singer and presenter Jordan Stephens, who has posted multiple TikToks criticising the franchise's return.And last month, discussing the film's trailer on the Jeremy Vine show, Labour MP Paulette Hamilton called the character racist. She said she believed Baron Cohen would not get away with portraying any other racial group "in the way he has done with the black community". The character of Ali G rose to fame through a series of deadpan TV interviews with figures including Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed and the Beckhams, from which catchphrases such as "Booyakasha" and "Is it because I is black?" entered popular culture.But some critics say these catchphrases have since been appropriated by others in a real-life context to mock black people and dismiss their concerns.Comedian Dane Baptiste, the first black British comic nominated for an Edinburgh Comedy Award, remembers hearing Ali G catchphrases everywhere during the character's noughties heyday. "A lot of the time, I would hear people using phrases like 'Is it because I is black?' or 'Booyakasha'," he recalls."Even taking the phrase 'Is it because I is black?'... that was used to the point of caricature, whereby, whenever black people experienced actual grievances relating to systemic and institutional racism, it was reduced to this catchphrase."Baptiste believes the character, which he calls a "black caricature", is returning at a time when black creatives are being "starved of opportunities". When Ali G first arrived on our screens, characters like him were far more common, says social psychologist Amy Kean. She argues they are no longer "culturally relevant"."Ali G, Little Britain, Catherine Tate, all of those comedians and sketch shows, they made the voice the joke," says Kean, who has written on accentism, drawing from her experiences being teased for her Essex accent."I remember going to school in the 90s and people would take the piss out of anyone whose voice wasn't exactly the same as everyone else's."Baron Cohen has in the past suggested that his character had a knack for pushing powerful interviewees into uncomfortable territory by playing with biases and expectations. Speaking on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert in 2020, Baron Cohen reflected on interviewing Donald Trump for Da Ali G Show, and recalled how the programme's producer was a well-spoken Englishman who Trump had assumed would be conducting the interview."I remember Donald Trump looking at me, and I'm wearing a sweatsuit," Baron Cohen said. "His face dropped. He was immediately furious that he was going to have to speak to somebody from a lower-class borough rather than this rather astute Etonian producer."When discussing the forthcoming sequel on CBS on Tuesday, Baron Cohen's "primary objective" appeared less ideological - to "get people to laugh really hard". Though he added that "smuggled in there is a bit of satire".In a new essay in Time this week, external, Baron Cohen argued that his characters have always been "vehicles to expose prejudice, bias, and stupidity", and that in the case of Ali G, "the joke is on him, and on the predominantly white male establishment" he aims to expose."The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him," Baron Cohen wrote."The world he's returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago. All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven't just lingered - they've metastasized. They're fueled by the greatest propaganda machine in history - social media - and now by its monstrous child, AI."The actor is no stranger to putting himself in potentially dangerous situations for his comedy. In a previous film, he infiltrated a gun rally, disguised as a "right-wing singer", while secretly wearing a bulletproof vest. Once members of the crowd realised they were being mocked, Baron Cohen was escorted into a getaway vehicle as an angry crowd "started pounding on the vehicle with their fists".Judging by Baron Cohen's description of the upcoming film, there may be further potential for danger. He told CBS he wanted to examine "conspiracies and lies" and test whether "we, in a matter of hours, could turn intelligent people who believed in the theory of race replacement into murderers".Colton Dunn, one of the film's black writers, questioned why Baron Cohen would put himself in danger, where interview subjects might react violently, if his intentions were racist. "From my point of view, Ali G is not a racist character. Ali G is a tool to expose racists," Dunn told Deadline."That's why I signed on. I wouldn't sign on to work with somebody that I thought was racist, that's against everything that I've done," he added.Almost 25 years on, Ali G still has loyal fans - including in his "home town" of Staines, in Surrey.Staines-upon-Thames resident Alex Balkan, who campaigned for a statue of Ali G in the town, says the character remains a source of local pride.While acknowledging not everyone welcomes the proposal, he says Ali G put Staines on the map."Everyone knows about us because of Ali G, and many of us wear that as a badge of pride," he says.  "It's a great conversation starter. It feels nice that people know about your town."Asked about accusations of racial stereotyping, Balkan believes the character is designed to be seen as a white man attempting to put on a stereotypical gangster persona, rather than to poke fun at black culture itself.One of the character's defenders is one of his most famous prank victims, politician Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg. "It is clever, satirical humour which makes the country, and many of us look foolish, and that's no bad thing," Sir Jacob posted on his social media. While some argue that audiences may have moved on from Ali G, supporters of the character contend that objections to his return reflect growing concerns about creative freedom in comedy. Balkan goes further, arguing that people today are more easily offended than they were two decades ago."This excessive zeal of political correctness, of left-wing po-facery, is crazy," Sir Jacob said. "It's a joke, it's comedy and it is poking fun at society as it is, as the best comedy often does."It would be unwise to judge the film before audiences have seen it. But the controversy surrounding its release suggests that, more than two decades after Ali G first appeared, the debate over who exactly is being laughed at is far from settled.

schema.headline: Ali G is back. But is Sacha Baron Cohen's character past its sell-by date?

title: What is happening with the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields?
description: If approved, Rosebank is expected to fill up to 500 million barrels of oil over its 25-year lifetime. But that increased supply does not necessarily g
body: If approved, Rosebank is expected to fill up to 500 million barrels of oil over its 25-year lifetime. But that increased supply does not necessarily guarantee cheaper energy bills for people in the UK. Prices are determined by international markets which are vulnerable to shocks such as the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran. Most of the oil produced from Rosebank would be sent to the Netherlands because the UK's remaining refineries are not equipped to process the heavier type of crude oil extracted from the North Sea.If any of the refined products - such as diesel or jet fuel - were to be used in the UK, they would then to be reimported.When plans for Jackdaw were unveiled in 2022, developers said it would produce enough gas to power 1.4 million homes.It would be a relatively simple process to connect Jackdaw to the UK energy system, meaning gas could be quickly pumped to the mainland.Announcing that the project would go ahead, the UK government said it was expected to increase domestic gas production by around 6% at its peak.It said that over its 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would protect hundreds of jobs and add an estimated £2.9bn to the UK economy.Backers say opening the fields would improve the UK's energy security.Yet Fatih Birol, a leading energy economist at the International Energy Agency, told The Guardian, external earlier this year that new drilling in the North Sea "would not change much for the UK's energy security" or bring down energy bills. He said that the UK would still be reliant on oil and gas imports, with prices set internationally. Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Norwegian company Equinor and Shell. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank. It has estimated that Jackdaw could produce 35.8 million tonnes of carbon over its lifetime, the equivalent of 90% of Scotland's emissions for 2023. Adura said a more likely estimate was about 23.6 million tonnes - equivalent to 60% of the 2023 figure. Those figures are dwarfed by the projections for Rosebank - almost 250 million tonnes of planet-warming emissions. Yet Adura's updated environmental impact assessment, ordered by the Court of Session, says that emissions from Jackdaw would "not materially influence" global warming.The firm says that displacing imported liquified nature gas from the United States with gas from the Jackdaw field would save the equivalent of four million tonnes of CO2. Campaign groups say that would not lower worldwide emissions as the US gas would still be sold and burned elsewhere. Adura also said the climate effects would be "minor" because the UK has a "well-regulated industry" aligned with the Paris Agreement, a legally binding commitment to limit global warming to between 1.5 and 2C.However, Greenpeace UK chief scientist Doug Parr said opening a new field was "wholly incompatible" with the Paris Agreement. Industry body Offshore Energies UK (OEUK) has said Rosebank and Jackdaw would support a peak of more than 3,500 jobs during the construction phase. It says the fields would support 880 jobs, external throughout during their lifespans, with an average salary of £85,850.OEUK also says they would provide £1.4bn in tax revenues by 2029, rising to £3.8bn  by 2034. Such figures are particularly attractive in the north-east of Scotland, which is contending with the decline of an industry which has long been its economic lifeblood. According to research for the UK Parliament, external, about four fifths of the oil and gas from British-controlled parts of the North Sea had been extracted by 2024. Campaign group Uplift says that trying to prop up the declining industry with the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields would only delay the transition to greener energy production, which it argues, external is needed to protect the environment and support jobs."The only way to protect workers, supply chain firms, and communities that are currently dependent on the oil and gas industry from this decline is to invest in renewables and other industries that have a long-term future," it says. Opening Rosebank and Jackdaw would deliver big profits for energy firms, and little benefit to taxpayers, Uplift adds. Ami McCarthy, head of politics at Greenpeace UK, said: "Trying to squeeze the last few drops of expensive oil and gas out of the North Sea while the world is reeling from climate impacts is beyond ridiculous."

schema.headline: What is happening with the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields?

title: Tighter rules planned to protect people from botched cosmetic surgery
description: The government began consulting on changes to the cosmetic surgery industry in 2023, but there have been calls for stricter regulations for many years
body: The government began consulting on changes to the cosmetic surgery industry in 2023, but there have been calls for stricter regulations for many years.It comes following horror stories of procedures reportedly carried out in Airbnbs, hotel rooms, garden sheds and even public toilets, by "cosmetic cowboys", external. Women have told the BBC of dangerous complications, pain and permanent scarring after treatment by rogue operators.Alice Webb, a mother-of-five from Gloucestershire, died within hours of getting a liquid Brazilian butt lift in 2024.That same year, Sasha Dean, from Bedfordshire, was left in a coma after receiving a liquid BBL. A BBL is a non-surgical cosmetic procedure in which dermal fillers are injected into the buttocks to alter their size or shape.Some of Sasha's treatment took place in a private house and she ended up developing sepsis.She told BBC News: "Very quickly it turned into a complete nightmare."I had a heart attack, one of my lungs had collapsed, my kidneys were failing. My body was just completely shutting down."Under the government's new rules:Fillers injected into parts of the body other than the face, like liquid BBLs, will be legally defined as cosmetic surgical procedures, meaning only doctors could perform the surgeryHigh-risk non-surgical or wellbeing treatments, including deep chemical peels, vampire facials, dermal micro-coring and some laser procedures would be restricted to doctors, dentists and some nurses, midwives and pharmacists who have been trainedCosmetic surgery and risky treatments will be banned for under 18s - lip fillers and face Botox on children has already been stoppedVampire facials involve drawing a patient's blood and then separating out platelet-rich plasma from it using a centrifuge. The plasma is then injected back into the face through tiny needle puncturesDermal micro-coring involves removing tiny sections of skin using thin hollow needles, small enough to allow scarless healingChemical peels are skin resurfacing procedures that use a chemical solution to remove the top layers of skinHealth Minister Karin Smyth said: "We want to drive cosmetic cowboys out of the market and raise standards across the board, giving reputable businesses a fair chance to thrive by helping people identify safe, qualified providers they can trust."The British Beauty Council said the government should be congratulated for tackling the issue head-on.But Mr Keith Allison, from the Royal College of Surgeons of England, said the consultation was "long overdue" and, while welcome, the proposals did not go far enough."Ministers must ensure they do not create a new loophole in patient protection by regulating non-surgical cosmetic procedures more robustly than cosmetic surgery itself."A doctor should not be able to carry out cosmetic surgery simply because they hold a medical license."The government will now ask doctors, businesses, regulators, the public and other experts for their say on the draft rules, before plans go through parliament in  spring 2027.A licensing scheme for Botox clinics in England to improve safety standards has already been announced.In Scotland, laws passed in March mean cosmetic procedures must be performed by, or alongside, certain healthcare professionals in a registered setting. Non-surgical procedures are banned for under 18s.There are no dedicated regulations around cosmetic procedures in Wales or Northern Ireland.

schema.headline: Tighter rules planned to protect people from botched cosmetic surgery

title: Missing German WW2 U-boat discovered off Devon 82 years on
description: Image source, GasperadosImage caption, The U-boat was scuttled by its own crew after it was attacked by the Royal Navy in July 1944ByJohnny Rutherford
body: Image source, GasperadosImage caption, The U-boat was scuttled by its own crew after it was attacked by the Royal Navy in July 1944ByJohnny Rutherford and Britta ZeltmannDevonA German submarine that went missing during World War Two after being damaged by the Royal Navy has been discovered 82 years on. Plymouth dive team Gasperados identified the U-672 about 20 miles (32km) off Salcombe, Devon, after it was discovered by a deep sea diving team from Portland in August at a depth of about 230ft (70m).The vessel was attacked by HMS Balfour in July 1944 but was scuttled by its 52 crew - all of whom survived. A navy log showing the sinking had incorrect coordinates, resulting in it not being found until recently. Members of Gasperados said they were "really pleased" they could help identify the vessel.Gasperados diver Dominic Robinson said: "Once we started moving around it and I started seeing the individual features - I saw the snorkel, I saw the conning tower, all those kind of things - I knew that we were going to get the video needed to identify it, so I was really pleased about that."After its attack, the U-boat was left leaking underwater.Its commander waited for as long as possible before making the decision to blow the tanks and bring the sub up to give its crew a last chance of survival.Robinson said they "managed to get it to the surface" before getting into their life rafts for survival."They were bobbing around in the sea and then the very next day they were found by British aircraft, British vessels and then taken away to the prisoner of war camp," he explained.Image source, GasperadosImage caption, Divers discovered the boat in August before it was officially identified German World War Two historian Dr Axel Niestle, who specialises in U-boats, said the wreck "was in the correct position" but, "due to a clerical error in the documents", had a position recorded which differed "some 46 miles (74km) from the actual position".The surviving crewmembers returned to Germany after the war, including the U-boat's skipper. Robinson said he had spoken to his family, who said he lived a "long and happy life".He added: "They just said how proud he would have been and how pleased he would have been to know that it had been found at last."Follow BBC Devon on X, external, Facebook, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to spotlight@bbc.co.uk, external.

title: Champions League sets new goals record this season
description: More teams, more games - and more goals.Since the current Champions League format was introduced at the start of the 2024-25 season, Europe's elite cl
body: More teams, more games - and more goals.Since the current Champions League format was introduced at the start of the 2024-25 season, Europe's elite club competition has delivered all of the above and more.Especially the goals part.Already trending upwards over the past two campaigns, there has been a genuine goals boom in this year's competition.The 187 goals scored so far have come at an average of 4.16 per game - the highest in Champions League history.Meanwhile, the average goals scored per game in the Premier League is 2.9, 3.03 in La Liga and 3.69 in the Bundesliga.There have also been no goalless draws yet in the Champions League."Look how many goals have been scored, it's phenomenal," ex-Manchester United and England winger Ashley Young said on BBC Radio 5 Live. "The attackers are being clinical."Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock described the volume of goals as "incredible" - so how unusual is it?Ever since Uefa announced its plans to alter the format of the Champions League in 2021, the impact on matches has been a hot topic. Scrutiny has only increased since the changes were implemented in time for the 2024-25 season.After beginning life as a six-team invitational tournament in 1955-56 before growing to a 32-team knockout tournament in 1967, the Champions League as we know it began in 1992.A group stage was added, with the last 16 entering a knockout phase. There was a brief spell with two group stages, but this was reverted back to the single group-stage format for the 2003-04 tournament.The group stage previously featured 32 teams in eight groups of four, with the top two sides from each of those groups qualifying for the last 16.For the start of the 2024-25 season, the group stage was replaced with a 36-team league phase, with each side playing eight one-off fixtures instead of six games against three teams.The top eight finishers qualify directly for the knockout stages, with those placed ninth to 24th entering a two-legged play-off stage.The bottom eight are eliminated, meaning that after eight matches, 24 sides are still in the competition. Some argue that that creates a lack of jeopardy, which encourages teams to play more expansively.But do more goals equal better quality? "I think the entertainment has gone up, although I'm not sure the quality has gone up," The Times football writer Tom Arnott told BBC Radio 5 Live."If I'm looking at the games it's brilliant to watch and thrilling because the football itself is fantastic - but what do they mean?"The lack of jeopardy, why would PSG and Barcelona play for a draw, why not go for it? If you need five wins from the eight games you know you've got some margin there. If you lose it's OK. I think the format allows all the teams to loosen up."The entertainment value is there but I think you come away from these matches sometimes and still think 'what does it all mean?'. The lack of jeopardy early on does deliver entertainment."

schema.headline: Champions League sets new goals record this season

title: Zelensky says intelligence sharing 'works now' as US envoy to meet Putin in Russia
description: Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks in Oslo alongside the Norwegian prime minister, said "genuine progress" had been ma
body: Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks in Oslo alongside the Norwegian prime minister, said "genuine progress" had been made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details, and warned that patience would be needed.Witkoff was not present at their joint press conference with Zelensky after the talks, nor was President Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner who had attended via video link. A US official later said the meeting had been "very productive and constructive" and that there was a "strong alignment at the working level" between the US, Ukraine and Europe on "next steps". Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that President Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.Speaking after the news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal".He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war".Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.Russian drone attacks have continued this week. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed on Tuesday - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.Another attack overnight on Wednesday killed two more people near Kharkiv, the country's second-largest city.Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now"."Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," he said.Zelensky also said he hoped for a good result on Starlink, after Ukraine's military had reported speed restrictions on drones using its internet network to conduct strikes against Russia.A bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into the restrictions last week.The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine had also been discussed, as well as energy ceasefire proposals, and restated that Kyiv was "ready for negotiations" to end the conflict. "Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said.Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre meanwhile stressed that Europe needed "to be at the table" during any discussions about how to bring the fighting to an end.Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine, but stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.European leaders have meanwhile expressed concern about recent US statements towards Russia.German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war on Monday, and said that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly"."It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy"."We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said.

schema.headline: Zelensky says intelligence sharing 'works now' as US envoy to meet Putin in Russia

title: Helen Haines: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says
description: Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirme
body: Helen Haines, the Australian MP who was hit by a car in what authorities say was a deliberate attack, has lost both her legs, her husband has confirmed.Phil Haines said the"horrendous incident" caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind are in good shape". He added that the "good news in all this is that she's alive".The alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, faces multiple charges and appeared in court for the first time on Wednesday.Nugent was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the independent MP outside her electorate office in the regional town of Wangaratta, about 240km (150miles) northeast of Melbourne.Haines' "road to recovery will be long and difficult, but we know she is a fighter," her husband said at a press conference in Melbourne where she is being treated. "She is a determined person who will do her best, with our support and love, to recover. And that is what we hope for."He thanked hospital staff and people, both in Australia and internationally, who have shown their concern for Haines, and urged those who want to show their support to donate to the Save the Children fund."Please keep sending Helen your love," he added.Earlier on Wednesday, Nugent appeared at the local court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges may be laid, including attempted murder.Nugent - a local from the nearby town of Tarrawingee and known as an environmental campaigner - remained silent and emotionless during his brief court appearance. He did not apply for bail and is due back in court in February. Court documents show he was also charged with cultivating and possessing cannabis.In court, Nugent's lawyer said that his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.The court also heard that Nugent has a rare neurological condition - idiopathic transverse myelitis - caused by inflammation of the spinal cord.Victoria Police said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police (AFP), remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established."His motivation for this - what we allege is a deliberate attack - is very much a centrepiece of the investigation," said Victoria Police Commissioner Mike Bush."Our people will continue to explore every element, angle and avenue to work that out. It's something that, when we work towards it, discover it, we will present in court."Nugent was not on the radar of police and there was no intelligence of any threat to Haines before the incident, police said.Investigators are also looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident and if there was any personal connection between Nugent and Haines.Nugent's family earlier put out a statement saying they were long-time friends with Haines, who is the independent MP for the regional seat of Indi in Victoria. They described the apparent attack as "devastating and unfathomable".The incident occurred on Monday afternoon at around 15.35, local time. Moments after the car hit Haines, bystanders pulled Nugent out of the vehicle and detained him.Jacob and Jackie Evans were among the first on the scene, and said Haines was grateful to them for coming to her aid as she lay severely injured. "Thank you, you lovely people," is what Haines said to them, according to the Herald Sun."She was thanking us, it was incredible," Jackie told Nine's Today programme.Jacob used a tourniquet he had in a medical kit in his car to help stem the bleeding from one of Haines's legs.Haines underwent surgery after the incident and lost one of her legs. As of Wednesday morning she has also lost the other leg, her husband Phil told reporters.The community in Wangaratta, as well as the wider political community, are in shock over the incident in a country where political violence is rare.Leaders from across the political spectrum have paid tribute to Haines, who was first elected in 2019 and is well regarded by her peers.Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had spoken to Haines's husband several times since the incident.In an interview with the national broadcaster ABC, Albanese said threats to female politicians were marked by a "different form of vilification and aggression" such as threats of rape.There has also been a recent growing trend of threats against "high office holders", with almost one person a week being charged for such offences, police said.Monday's incident has sparked debate over the level of security for MPs.Federal police said that individual protection for every one of the country's 226 federal MPs would require "incredible" levels of staffing.Instead, police assess the need for close personal protection based on a person's role and the threat environment around them, police said.Australia's Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who spoke at the same press conference as Haines' husband, said this was "a moment for us to pause, and to choose to be better". "We should do what I imagine Helen would be doing if she was not the victim of this terrible attack - reaching out to those who are terribly distressed by what has happened," she says."Most importantly, that we learn or re-learn to exercise our muscle of decency."

schema.headline: Helen Haines: Australian MP loses both legs after alleged car attack, husband says

title: Tesla and SpaceX: Why does Elon Musk want to merge the companies?
description: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?Image source, Getty Images/ReutersByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 2 hours agoElon Mu
body: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?Image source, Getty Images/ReutersByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 2 hours agoElon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.How likely is the merger?"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group.The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.Figure caption, Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said. But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added."There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%.What would it mean for customers?Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models.Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said. "The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added.The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights.The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January.What does Musk get out of it? The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year.The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider.A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said."The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said.However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month. Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn."I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said. The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

schema.headline: Tesla and SpaceX: Why does Elon Musk want to merge the companies?

title: France is divided over who to blame for weekend riots
description: "This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us
body: "This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October. I'd stopped Elisabeth and her friend to ask their thoughts on what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears."My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.The president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend. French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black, folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left. It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections. LFI denies this.The mass looting of what is said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity?Emmanuel Macron, who is on his way out as president and viewed by many in France as a lame duck, and his government are accused of dropping the ball and failing to keep the country safe on Saturday.Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice.Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts have led former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence. Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's interior minister, Bernard Quintin, warned of the "TikTokisation" of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liège on "known far-left groups".In France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire", said Nuñez. On Tuesday Lecornu spoke of  "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups". Previously he had accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos. It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied.Mélenchon took part in Saturday's planned protest. Politicians from his LFI movement have been present at the student demonstrations since they started a month ago in the socially deprived outskirts of Paris, with demands for better state education for all.In Saint-Denis suburb on Monday, I met Lisa Cordat, of the FSE student union. She told me that students had organised themselves for demos via social media messaging or through student-led organisations. She said it was "insulting" to suggest they were being manipulated or "told to do this, or do that" by politicians. "Student anger comes from the ground up," says Lisa.But there is also a palpable frustration amongst many in France at what they see as the politicisation of Saturday's violence. Lina, who is 25, told me: "Politicians are hunting for scapegoats but don't ask why it all happened. The root causes of Saturday. We feel scared and abandoned."France's leading politicians have indulged in a festival of finger-pointing since Saturday.The presidential election here in six months' time is hotly contested and the volatility on French streets funneled immediately into France's already febrile politics.Mélenchon, currently running in second place in most polls, ahead of centrist candidates, accused France's centrist prime minister of being "responsible for the chaos" either due to "incompetence or a worst-case strategy." Mélenchon went on to apparently imply Lecornu may have allowed the violence to unfold, so as to position itself as a "party of order", after Saturday's lawlessness, "that would make people forget his failure in public finances".France is struggling with spiralling public debt and government borrowing costs.As for intelligence failures on Saturday, President Macron has demanded explanations and a new policing strategy. France's interior minister admitted there were not enough officers on the streets, despite the nationwide protests being publicised well in advance. Following accusations of heavy-handedness at earlier demos, the police seemed very much out of their depth this weekend.Of all the presidential hopefuls, it would seem Marine Le Pen of the anti-immigration National Rally party gains most politically from Saturday's shocking scenes.She is already way ahead in opinion polls. Le Pen chose to launch a presidential-looking video address to the nation via social media on Sunday. Dressed formally, behind a large desk and in front of a French flag, she blamed Jean-Luc Mélenchon by name for his associates who "look to throw the country into chaos," she said. She also accused the Macron government of "running out of steam", meaning that France was "taken hostage between violence and powerlessness". She ended her video by reminding French voters they would have the opportunity to "choose a different path" in six months' time.Le Pen's party promotes a law and order, closed-border message and, like US President Donald Trump and US Vice President JD Vance, has blamed migrants, amongst others, for the chaos in France on Saturday. French authorities have not implicated migrants in the violence.One teacher called Mar complained that Saturday's violence "suits politicians' purpose. It distracts from weeks of legitimate protests for better public services", she said. "Politicians aren't listening to what the students need, or what teachers need or what the French people want. They're using the violence to election-campaign to become president and to try to make their opponents look bad."But increasing numbers in France, many amongst the young Gen Z generation, say they have dwindling faith in "the system". That's something we see echoed in other European countries where mainly youth-led protests erupted - some violently - this weekend in Italy, Portugal and Albania as well as France and Belgium. These demonstrations are often triggered by spiralling living costs, deteriorating public services and a sense of powerlessness people feel over their own lives. What can we do as individuals about our rising energy costs caused by wars far away in the Middle East or in Ukraine, many ask. Voters increasingly say they are losing faith in traditional or governing political parties to listen to concerns and address them. The young look at climate change, social inequality, impossible housing prices and AI potentially threatening their place in the job market.According to opinion polls conducted by this year by Pew, 69% of people in France are dissatisfied with democracy. In Spain, it's 68% and in Italy, 62%. The US is experiencing similar disillusionment with 69% saying they are dissatisfied with how democracy is working.So many people I've spoken to in France since Saturday's riots emphasise the importance in making a clear distinction between angry but peaceful protesters, and those intent on wreaking violent havoc.Politics aside, is what we're now seeing in Europe's protest wave perhaps a powerful cocktail of a bubbling over of frustration, cries for help for the authorities to listen but also, for some, a dark sense there's little left to lose?

schema.headline: France is divided over who to blame for weekend riots

title: I left top secret files on the train - you can recover from the biggest mistake of your life
description: Warning: This story contains a reference to suicideIt was an ordinary Tuesday train ride to work when top civil servant Richard Jackson made the bigge
body: Warning: This story contains a reference to suicideIt was an ordinary Tuesday train ride to work when top civil servant Richard Jackson made the biggest mistake of his life. By the time he realised, with a sudden jolt of panic, it was too late.He had left highly classified documents on the train.The split-second error became national news and Jackson's life was thrown into turmoil. He was consumed by shame and humiliation.Nearly 20 years on, he recounts that fateful day and the aftermath to BBC Radio 4's Life Changing podcast. He says he is proof that even when you've made your worst mistake you can rebuild your life.Before his life unravelled, Jackson was 37 and living in Yateley in Hampshire with wife Maddie and stepdaughter Charlotte, 15. His other stepdaughter Becky, 20, was at university."We were very happy," he says. "But I was very focused on my career."My worth and my value came from that career, job title, position and responsibility."I found myself working 100-hour weeks for a while," he says. "I didn't switch off."He had been seconded from the Ministry of Defence to the Cabinet Office for a job in global terrorism, handling first-hand intelligence from GCHQ, MI5 and MI6.Leaving his Whitehall office one Monday evening, he swept up a pile of forms to fill in to make his secondment official.Back at home, he realised that buried within the bundle were "two papers on two classified subjects, and they were both top secret".Jackson hid away at home. One lunchtime, Maddie found him sitting cross-legged on the sofa sobbing. "I'd spent the morning trying to find a painless way to die," he says, "I've often thought what would have happened if she hadn't come home that lunchtime… but I guess I'll never know. "We spent that afternoon talking… and I think that was the first time where I thought, 'if I'm going to get through this, I can't do it on my own'."The Cabinet Office found it was an act of gross misconduct and demoted him three grades. He was charged under the Official Secrets Act, avoided jail, and was fined £2,500.On paper it was over. But Jackson could not shake the feelings of shame, regret and humiliation. He credits the many people who cared about him for helping him piece his life back together. "I fixed very little myself. Lots of people fixed me."After returning to the MoD in an HR role, then moving to the Department for Culture, Media and Sport to work on the Olympics, Jackson left the Civil Service and worked for the Samaritans. He then took on a role running a team of analysts looking at global terror risk, and started training as a life coach in his spare time.When he was made redundant, he set up a coaching company, NewDay, which helps people cope with the stress of handling distressing material."I could tell my story... and there'd be a point to it. There'd be a reason for what I did."Richard Jackson has shared steps that helped him move through his traumatic episode: Get your thoughts out of your head. In a dark place, your mind jumps from "I made a terrible mistake" to "I am a worthless person" at the speed of thought. Writing it down or talking to someone slows things down to give you a chance to notice the illogical leaps.Continue activities you enjoy. When you feel unworthy, you stop doing the things that lift you up. Work out what they are - the gym, a book, a long walk - and make them non-negotiable fixtures in your routine.Remember your worth and your success. I keep an evidence board by my desk with notes of things I have achieved and kind things people have said. It's a tangible reminder that I am not that mistake, I am so much more.Find your critical friend. You need someone who is your cheerleader but will also call you out when you let good habits slip. Anyone who is truly on your side.Work out what you can fix, and what you can't. If you've caused harm, take responsibility: apologise and put things right where you can. But don't assume responsibility for things that were never yours to carry.Don't confuse your worst moment with the whole story of your life. You are not that mistake. You are still the person who existed before it, and there can still be a person after it whom you haven't met.If you or someone you know has been affected by a traumatic experience or is suffering from emotional distress, there is support on the BBC Action Line website.

schema.headline: I left top secret files on the train - you can recover from the biggest mistake of your life
